isle-of-pines: The Isle of Pines, white rum shaken with grapefruit, mint and sugar, is a Havana-style sour named after the island off Cuba's southern coast now called the Isla de la Juventud, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.
gin-blossom: The Gin Blossom is credited to Julie Reiner, who served it at the Clover Club, the bar she opened in Brooklyn's Cobble Hill in 2008 after making her name at the Flatiron Lounge in Manhattan. She built it as a stirred drink in the Martini mould, gin with vermouth and orange bitters. Its trick is the eau-de-vie, an unsweetened apricot brandy that brings the scent of the fruit without the sugar a liqueur would add, so the drink stays dry.
industry-sour: The Industry Sour, Fernet-Branca and green Chartreuse shaken with lime and sugar, is named for the bar trade, which calls itself the industry, and published credits for its creation disagree, so who first made it is not settled.
trident: The Trident is the work of Robert Hess, the Seattle drinks writer and educator who published as DrinkBoy, and it dates from around 2000. Hess built it as an experiment in rebuilding the Negroni from different parts, keeping the classic's equal measures of spirit, bitter and fortified wine and swapping each one: aquavit for gin, Cynar for Campari and dry sherry for vermouth. It was created to use Fee Brothers' peach bitters, which still finish it.
slope: The Slope is credited to Julie Reiner, the New York bartender behind the Flatiron Lounge in Manhattan and the Clover Club in Brooklyn, and it is a Manhattan variation of rye with Punt e Mes and a little apricot liqueur. It takes its name from Park Slope, and it belongs with the drinks named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods that New York bartenders made in the 2000s, beginning with the Red Hook at Milk & Honey.
fort-washington-flip: The Fort Washington Flip, applejack and maple syrup shaken with a whole egg, is a modern American take on the old whole-egg flip, and the bartender who created it and the reason for its name are not reliably recorded.
coffee-flip: The Coffee Flip, cold coffee and tawny port shaken with a whole egg, has no recorded creator, and it adds real coffee to the old Coffee Cocktail of port, brandy and egg, which Jerry Thomas admitted was named only for how it looked in the glass.
scorpion: The Scorpion is one of Victor Bergeron's signature drinks, served at the Trader Vic's restaurants that grew out of his Oakland bar, and his books of the 1940s print it, including a version for a group served in a bowl. That bowl of rum, brandy, orgeat and citrus, with a gardenia floating in the middle, became one of the emblems of the tiki era. When Bergeron first mixed it, and why he called it the Scorpion, are not recorded.
q-b-cooler: The Q.B. Cooler comes from Don the Beachcomber, the Hollywood bar that Ernest Gantt, later known as Donn Beach, opened in the 1930s and from which the tiki drink grew. Its rums, honey, ginger and citrus became part of the Mai Tai quarrel: a longtime colleague said Beach's claim to the Mai Tai really meant that Trader Vic's drink was modelled on the Q.B. Cooler, and drinks historians still argue over how alike the two are. The initials are usually said to stand for the Quiet Birdmen, a fraternity of aviators.
ancient-mariner: Jeff Berry, the tiki historian known as Beachbum Berry, created the Ancient Mariner in 1994 and published it in his first book, the Grog Log, in 1998, while he was tracking down the lost recipes of Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic. He built it to taste like a drink from those original Polynesian bars, with Demerara and Jamaican rums, grapefruit, lime and allspice. The name borrows the title of Coleridge's poem, and the drink has become a modern tiki standard.
brace-up: The Brace Up survives in a later edition of the bar guide by Jerry Thomas, the New York bartender whose book was the first widely circulated American bartender's guide; it is not in his first edition. It shakes brandy with a whole egg, lemon, sugar and a touch of anise, and its name reads like an instruction to pull yourself together. Thomas gathered many of his recipes from other bars, so who first mixed it is not recorded.
jersey-cocktail: The Jersey Cocktail appears in Jerry Thomas's How to Mix Drinks of 1862, the first widely circulated American bartender's guide, among cocktails built on the old formula of a base, sugar and bitters. Thomas fills the glass with cider, mixed with sugar and bitters and finished with lemon peel, and the drink is generally taken to be named for New Jersey, whose orchards supplied much of the cider and applejack drunk in the northeast. Its inventor is not recorded.
hot-spiced-rum: Hot rum drinks were a winter staple of colonial New England, where rum distilled from Caribbean molasses was the everyday spirit. Jerry Thomas fixed this one in print in 1862: Jamaica rum, sugar, a spoonful of allspice and cloves, a piece of butter as large as half a chestnut and a tumbler topped up with hot water. The name simply describes the drink, and the Hot Buttered Rum most people now order is the same idea with the butter promoted to the title.
champagne-cobbler: Jerry Thomas's How to Mix Drinks of 1862 printed a Champagne Cobbler alongside sherry, catawba, hock and claret versions, applying the cobbler of wine, sugar and fruit over shaved ice to sparkling wine. The cobbler family had swept American bars in the decades before, and Charles Dickens put the sherry version in Martin Chuzzlewit. Thomas says the Champagne Cobbler should be sipped through a straw, and the cobbler helped make the straw a bar fixture. Its creator is not recorded.
port-cobbler: The Port Cobbler is the nineteenth-century American cobbler of wine, sugar and fruit churned over crushed ice made with port, one of many variations on the far more famous sherry cobbler, and no creator is recorded for it.
gin-smash: The smash is a nineteenth-century American drink, and Jerry Thomas's How to Mix Drinks of 1862 gives brandy, gin and whiskey versions, describing it as simply a julep on a small plan. The difference was size: spirit, sugar and mint over shaved ice in a short glass rather than a tall one, which is why old bar books treat the two as one family. The smash faded in the twentieth century and returned with the classic-cocktail revival.
santinas-pousse-cafe: Joseph Santini, who ran a celebrated bar on Gravier Street in New Orleans in the 1850s, is remembered for two drinks: the Brandy Crusta and this pousse-café. Jerry Thomas printed it in 1862 as Santina's Pousse Café, crediting the proprietor of Santina's Saloon, a celebrated Spanish café in New Orleans, and the misspelling has stuck. Its brandy, maraschino and curaçao are now usually floated in three bands, and layering works on density, which follows sugar rather than alcohol, so the sweetest liqueur goes in first.
pousse-cafe: Pousse-café is French for coffee-pusher, and the name first belonged to any small after-dinner drink taken with or after coffee. In nineteenth-century New Orleans and New York it came to mean something more theatrical: liqueurs and spirits floated in separate coloured bands, poured slowly so that each settled on the one below. Jerry Thomas's guide of 1862 already printed several, including Santina's from New Orleans, and the drink became a test of a bartender's steady hand.
angels-kiss: The Angel's Kiss in its modern form, crème de cacao under a float of cream, is the simplest of the layered pousse-café drinks, and older books such as the Savoy Cocktail Book give the name to a four-band drink and print this two-band one as the Angel's Tip, with no creator recorded.
widows-dream: The Widow's Dream is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as a liqueur glass of Bénédictine shaken with a whole egg and topped with cream. Bénédictine was launched at Fécamp in Normandy in the 1860s by the merchant Alexandre Le Grand, who presented it as the revival of a lost recipe from the town's old Benedictine abbey, a story historians doubt. The cocktail's creator is not recorded, and neither is the widow of its title.
rock-and-rye: Rock and rye began in nineteenth-century American saloons as rye whiskey sweetened with crystallised rock candy, often with orange, lemon or other fruit added to the bottle. It was widely sold with claims that it eased coughs and colds, and bottled versions sat on pharmacy shelves as well as behind bars. No single inventor is recorded, and several small producers have since revived the bottled style.
barbados-rum-punch: Barbados is one of the places where rum began: planters there were distilling spirit from sugar-cane molasses by the mid-1600s, and English visitors called it kill-devil. Punch, a mix of spirit, citrus, sugar, water and spice that English sailors are thought to have picked up in India, became the island's way of drinking it. The traditional Barbadian rhyme is a mnemonic for the proportions rather than a list of ingredients, which is why the recipe scales to any size of bowl.
caudle: Caudle is one of the oldest drinks in English cookery, a warm mixture of wine or ale thickened with grain or egg yolks and sweetened, with recipes surviving from medieval cookbooks. Its name comes through Old French from the Latin for warm. For centuries it was a drink of the sickroom and the lying-in chamber, served to new mothers and to the visitors who came to see the baby. Its relative the posset was a richer dish of milk curdled with wine or ale.
french-76: The French 76 is a vodka version of the French 75, the gin, lemon and Champagne drink named after the French army's 75mm field gun of the First World War, with its number moved one step on, and no creator or bar of origin is recorded.
french-125: The French 125 rebuilds the French 75, named after the French army's 75mm field gun, on cognac instead of gin, a spirit some early recipes for the original already used, and who first gave the cognac version its own name is not recorded.
agavoni: The Agavoni, also called the Tequila Negroni, keeps the Negroni's equal measures of Campari and sweet vermouth and swaps gin for blanco tequila, its name a contraction of agave and Negroni, and its creator and date are not recorded.
tequila-sour: The Tequila Sour applies the old bar template of spirit, citrus and sugar, here with lemon and often egg white, to the agave spirit of Jalisco, and nobody has a documented claim to the first one.
mezcal-sour: The Mezcal Sour applies the classic sour of spirit, citrus and sugar to Oaxaca's mezcal, whose smoke comes from agave hearts roasted in earthen pits, and no single bartender is credited with the first one.
toreador: The Toreador is printed in the Café Royal Cocktail Book, compiled by W. J. Tarling for the United Kingdom Bartenders' Guild and published in London in 1937, alongside the Picador, another drink named for the bullring. Both belong to the handful of tequila drinks in British bar books of the period, when the spirit was still a rarity outside Mexico. Pairing tequila with apricot brandy and lime made a drink in the style of the era's fruit-brandy sours.
matador: The Matador, tequila shaken with pineapple and lime, has no recorded creator, and it is a different drink from the Matador of tequila, curaçao and dry vermouth printed in London's Café Royal Cocktail Book before the Second World War.
brave-bull: The Brave Bull is the tequila relative of the Black Russian, tequila poured over ice with coffee liqueur, its name a nod to the fighting bulls of the bullring, and who first made it, and where, is not recorded.
chapala: The Chapala, tequila with orange, lime, grenadine and a few drops of orange flower water, is named after Lake Chapala in Jalisco, Mexico's largest lake, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.
bertas-special: Berta's Special is linked to Bar Berta, a cantina on the main square of Taxco, the silver-mining town in Guerrero, beside the church of Santa Prisca. Its house drink of tequila with lime and honey, lengthened with soda, is known locally simply as a Berta and was taken up by visitors to the town. When the bar first poured it, and who the Berta of its name was, are not reliably recorded.
picador: The Picador appears in the Café Royal Cocktail Book, compiled by W. J. Tarling for the United Kingdom Bartenders' Guild and published in London in 1937. Its tequila, triple sec and lime use the same proportions as the Margarita, years before the Margarita became famous under its own name. Drinks historians cite it as evidence that the formula existed before the many bartenders and socialites who later claimed to have invented the Margarita. A picador is the mounted lancer of the bullfight.
cadillac-margarita: The Cadillac Margarita is the premium Margarita of reposado tequila with a float of Grand Marnier, named after the American car that became shorthand for the top of the range, and it has no recorded creator.
changuirongo: The Changuirongo is Mexico's everyday tequila highball, tequila topped with whatever soda is to hand, a cantina standby in Jalisco whose colloquial name has no documented origin.
jack-and-coke: The Jack and Coke pairs two Southern American brands, Jack Daniel's Tennessee whiskey from Lynchburg and Coca-Cola from Atlanta, and no one is credited with first pouring them together.
rum-and-coke: Rum and cola without the lime has no recorded inventor, while the version with lime is the Cuba Libre, which by most accounts began in Havana around the turn of the twentieth century, and the Andrews Sisters' wartime hit Rum and Coca-Cola made the pairing famous across the United States.
whiskey-ginger: The Whiskey Ginger, whiskey lengthened with ginger ale, has no recorded inventor, and with a squeeze of lemon or lime it becomes a buck, an older and better documented family of highballs.
vodka-cranberry: The Vodka Cranberry is the Cape Codder without its lime, a pairing the Ocean Spray cranberry growers' cooperative promoted from the mid-twentieth century and later named after the cranberry bogs of Massachusetts, and it has no single inventor.
vodka-soda: The Vodka Soda is the plainest of highballs, vodka lengthened with soda water, with no inventor or birthplace, and it became a standard order as vodka spread through American bars after the Second World War.
vodka-tonic: The Vodka Tonic is the Gin and Tonic with vodka in the gin's place, a highball that followed vodka into Western bars after the Second World War, and it has no recorded creator.
tequila-and-tonic: Tequila and Tonic is a simple highball of blanco tequila and tonic water, made wherever the agave spirit of Jalisco is poured, and no bartender or bar has a documented claim to it.
dogs-nose: Dog's Nose is an old English mixture of beer and gin, and one of its earliest appearances in print is in Charles Dickens's The Pickwick Papers, serialised from 1836. In the novel a temperance society's report records a tailor's fondness for it, describing the drink as warm porter, moist sugar, gin and nutmeg. The origin of the name is not documented, and the mixture belongs to the long English pub habit of strengthening beer with spirit.
flaming-dr-pepper: The Flaming Dr Pepper takes its name from the soft drink first served in Waco, Texas, though it contains none: amaretto under a lit layer of high-strength spirit, dropped into beer, is meant to recall the soda's flavour, and the almond against the malt comes surprisingly close. The best-known claim to have invented it comes from Dave Brinks of the Gold Mine Saloon in New Orleans, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.
blow-job: The Blow Job is an innuendo-named American novelty shot of coffee liqueur and Irish cream under whipped cream, traditionally lifted without using hands, and nobody has a documented claim to inventing it.
white-gummy-bear: The White Gummy Bear is a modern American shot of vodka, peach schnapps, sour mix and lemon-lime soda named after the sweet it imitates, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.
chocolate-cake-shot: The Chocolate Cake Shot, hazelnut liqueur and vodka chased with a sugared lemon wedge, contains no chocolate and takes its name from the cake-like taste the combination leaves, and it has no recorded creator.
melon-ball: The Melon Ball, Midori with vodka and pineapple, has no recorded creator and rose with the melon liqueur itself, which Suntory launched in the United States with a party at Studio 54 in New York in the late 1970s.
ferrari-shot: The Ferrari Shot, equal parts Fernet-Branca and Campari, is a bartenders' pour associated with San Francisco's devotion to Fernet, its name usually explained by its red colour, and it has no recorded inventor.
sourtoe-cocktail: The Sourtoe Cocktail began in 1973 in Dawson City, Yukon, when Captain Dick Stevenson, a local riverboat captain, turned a preserved human toe into a club initiation. The toe, the story goes, had belonged to a rum-runner of the 1920s who lost it to frostbite. The ritual is now run at the Downtown Hotel's Sourdough Saloon, where the rule is that the toe must touch the drinker's lips, and after a guest deliberately swallowed one in 2013 the fine for doing so was raised to 2,500 Canadian dollars.
blue-motorcycle: The Blue Motorcycle is one of the many offshoots of the Long Island Iced Tea, swapping the cola for blue curaçao and lemon-lime soda over the same five-spirit base, and its own creator is not recorded.
trash-can: The Trash Can is a recent American party drink built on the Long Island Iced Tea's five spirits with blue curaçao, served with a can of energy drink upended into the glass, and it has no recorded creator.
banana-daiquiri: The Banana Daiquiri is one of the blended fruit daiquiris that grew from the frozen Daiquiri made famous at Havana's El Floridita by Constantino Ribalaigua Vert in the 1930s, and no one is recorded as the first to add banana.
strawberry-daiquiri: The Strawberry Daiquiri descends from the frozen daiquiris of Havana's El Floridita, blending strawberries into the rum, lime and sugar original, and it became a fixture of American restaurants and resort bars without any recorded creator.
frose: Frosé, a contraction of frozen rosé, is credited to Bar Primi in New York, which put a blended frozen rosé on its menu in the summer of 2016. It spread across the United States within a season, helped by photographs shared online and by rosé's rising popularity. The method relies on alcohol lowering the wine's freezing point, so rosé left in a freezer sets into a slush rather than a solid block and blends easily with fruit and lemon.
amaretto-stone-sour: The Amaretto Stone Sour is amaretto in a stone sour, the American sour lengthened with orange juice and sometimes called a California sour, and no bartender is credited with it.
brandy-ice: The Brandy Ice, brandy and crème de cacao blended with vanilla ice cream, is an American after-dinner drink in the line of the Brandy Alexander, with the cream swapped for ice cream, and no creator or bar of origin is recorded.
bombardino: The Bombardino comes from Livigno, a ski town in the Italian Alps near the Swiss border, and its origin story is told in more than one way. In the most often told version a man from Genoa running the Mottolino mountain hut served the hot mix to skiers coming in from a blizzard, and one of them said it was like a little bomb, which gave it its name. Another account credits Aldo Del Bò, a local ski-lift manager, in 1972. Either way, it spread from Livigno to ski resorts across northern Italy.
campari-spritz: The Campari Spritz is the Veneto's spritz of sparkling wine, bitter liqueur and soda made with Campari, the Milanese bitter that is stronger and sharper than Aperol, and like most spritz variations it has no recorded creator.
rabarbaro-spritz: The Rabarbaro Spritz swaps the usual orange bitter in the Veneto's spritz for rabarbaro, the Milanese style of rhubarb-root amaro best known through Rabarbaro Zucca, and the serve has no recorded creator.
braulio-spritz: The Braulio Spritz puts Braulio, the alpine amaro of Bormio named after the Braulio valley where its herbs were first gathered, in place of Aperol or Campari, and the serve has no recorded creator.
limoncello-spritz: The Limoncello Spritz is a recent southern Italian take on the Veneto's spritz built on limoncello, the lemon-zest liqueur whose birthplace Capri, Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast all claim, and it has no single creator.
prairie-oyster: The Prairie Oyster belongs to the Victorian and Edwardian tradition of morning-after restoratives, and its name is a joke: the whole raw yolk, swallowed unbroken, stands in for an oyster on a prairie about as far from the sea as one can get. Harry Craddock printed a version in the Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and P. G. Wodehouse's valet Jeeves, whose own restorative is a similar mixture, gave the type its most famous fictional outing. Its creator is not recorded.
bull-shot: The Bull Shot is usually credited to the Caucus Club in Detroit, where it is said to have been created in the early 1950s by mixing vodka with cold beef bouillon in place of the Bloody Mary's tomato juice. It became a fashionable lunchtime and brunch drink of the late 1950s and 1960s, a savoury sibling of the Bloody Mary, served hot as well as cold. Canned beef consommé made it easy for any bar to reproduce.
ojen-cocktail: Ojén is an anise liqueur named after the Andalusian town near Málaga where it was first distilled, and New Orleans took it up so thoroughly in the nineteenth century that it became one of the city's Carnival drinks, poured at Mardi Gras gatherings as the Ojen Frappé or the Ojen Cocktail. When the Spanish producer stopped making it late in the twentieth century, the city's bars made their remaining bottles last as long as they could, and the Sazerac Company, based in New Orleans, later revived the liqueur for its home market.
vodka-martini: The Vodka Martini spread in the 1950s, when vodka was rising fast in American and British bars and many drinkers wanted a Martini without gin's botanicals; early versions were sometimes called the Kangaroo. Ian Fleming, writing in London, helped make it famous by having James Bond order his vodka Martinis shaken and not stirred, a phrase the films turned into a catchphrase. Bartenders still mostly stir it, since shaking clouds the drink and adds more water. No single bartender is credited with the first one.
fifty-fifty: The Fifty-Fifty, equal parts gin and dry vermouth, is printed under that name in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, but the proportions were not new: Martini and Martinez recipes of the late nineteenth century often used as much vermouth as gin, or more. Over the following decades the gin share kept climbing until the dry Martini became almost neat spirit, which is why the even split now reads as a revival. Bartenders of the classic-cocktail revival brought it back as the 50/50 Martini, often with orange bitters, as a lighter and more aromatic drink.
tuxedo-no-2: The Tuxedo takes its name from the Tuxedo Club at Tuxedo Park, the private enclave founded by New York society in the 1880s, where the drink is said to have first been mixed; the same club is credited with giving the tailless dinner jacket its American name. A close relative of the early Martini, it was built on gin and dry vermouth seasoned with a few dashes of liqueur and bitters. As bar books multiplied, so did Tuxedo recipes, and later guides numbered them to tell the versions apart. Who first mixed it at the club is not recorded.
reverse-manhattan: The Reverse Manhattan flips the classic's proportions so that sweet vermouth is the base and rye the accent, the same move as the Reverse Martini, and no individual is credited with the first one.
sherry-julep: The Sherry Julep applies the nineteenth-century American julep of spirit, sugar and mint over crushed ice to sherry, the wine of the fashionable sherry cobbler, and its creator is not recorded.
vermouth-cassis: Vermouth Cassis, dry French vermouth with crème de cassis and a splash of soda, is a French café aperitif also known as a Pompier, French for fireman, a nickname whose reason is not documented, and it has no recorded creator.
cynar-negroni: The Cynar Negroni puts Cynar, the Italian artichoke amaro launched in the years after the Second World War, in Campari's place in the Negroni's equal measures with gin and sweet vermouth, and no creator is recorded for the swap.
dukes-martini: Dukes Bar, in a hotel tucked into St James's in London, built its reputation on a Martini served without ice: gin and glasses kept in the freezer, the glass rinsed with vermouth and the gin poured in at the table. Salvatore Calabrese, who ran the bar in the 1980s, is credited with making the frozen style its signature, and his successors kept it. The bar's lore holds that Ian Fleming drank there and that it shaped Bond's taste in Martinis. Because the undiluted drink is so strong, staff decline to serve any guest more than two.
connaught-martini: The Connaught Martini belongs to the Connaught Bar in Mayfair, which opened in its present form in 2008 inside the Connaught hotel, in a room designed by David Collins. Under Agostino Perrone the bar turned the Martini into table-side theatre: a trolley is wheeled to the guest, the spirit is chosen, a selection of the bar's own bitters is offered, and the drink is stirred and poured in front of the guest. The ritual has become the bar's signature and one of the most recognisable Martini services in London.
havana-cocktail: The Havana Cocktail is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, the collection compiled at the American Bar of the Savoy hotel in London. Despite its name it contains no rum: apricot brandy and gin are joined by Swedish punsch, a Scandinavian liqueur built on Batavia arrack that was a common bar ingredient between the wars. Craddock did not explain the name, and many Savoy drinks were named after people, places or events now forgotten. Punsch's later disappearance from English-speaking bars left the drink obscure for decades.
thistle: The Thistle is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and it is effectively the same drink as the Rob Roy, which was created at the Waldorf Hotel in New York in 1894 and named after an operetta. The Thistle takes its name from Scotland's national emblem, which legend links to Norse raiders who are said to have given away a night attack by crying out after stepping barefoot on thistles. Its creator is not recorded.
flying-scotsman: Harry Craddock printed this drink in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as the Flying Scotchman, a sweetened Scotch and vermouth cocktail named after the famous express train between London King's Cross and Edinburgh. The service had been running since the 1860s, and the locomotive given the same name became a national celebrity: in 1934 it was the first steam locomotive officially recorded at one hundred miles an hour. The drink is a sweeter relation of the Rob Roy, and its creator is not recorded.
pineapple-fizz: The Pineapple Fizz appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, one of the simplest fizzes in the book: rum, pineapple and sugar shaken and lengthened with soda. The fizz family itself is American, taking shape in the later nineteenth century as sours lengthened with soda water. Pineapple had long been a status symbol in Britain, and in the eighteenth century the fruit was so rare and costly that it was sometimes hired rather than bought, to decorate a dinner table. The drink's creator is not recorded.
carroll-gardens: The Carroll Gardens is credited to Joaquín Simó, who created it at Death & Co in New York in 2008, one of the drinks named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods that followed the Red Hook from Milk & Honey. It pairs rye with Punt e Mes, Amaro Nardini and a touch of maraschino, an Italian accent on the old Brooklyn formula. Like the rest of the series it works around the original Brooklyn's Amer Picon, a French bitter aperitif that is not sold in the United States.
cobble-hill: The Cobble Hill was created by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York, one of the run of Brooklyn-cocktail variations named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods that began at the same bar with the Red Hook. Ross, the Australian-born bartender also known for the Penicillin and the Paper Plane, built it on rye with dry vermouth, the floral Amaro Montenegro and muddled cucumber, which gives it a cool, green note none of the other variations share.
bushwick: The Bushwick is usually credited to Phil Ward at Death & Co in New York, one of the drinks that bartenders there named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods in the 2000s, and it stays closest to the drink they all descend from. The original Brooklyn, a pre-Prohibition mix of rye, vermouth, maraschino and Amer Picon, faded because the French bitter is not sold in the United States. Bars making the Bushwick track down a bottle of Picon, use a house-made version or substitute an amaro.
la-ultima-palabra: La Última Palabra, Spanish for the last word, rebuilds the equal-parts Last Word of gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino and lime on mezcal instead of gin, and no single bartender is credited with naming it.
coffee-grog: The Coffee Grog, hot coffee with rum, a spiced butter batter and a flamed citrus peel, is a hot drink in the tiki style, and the bar that first served it is not reliably recorded.
sonic: The Sonic is a Japanese bar term joining soda and tonic, for a whisky or shochu highball lengthened with an even mix of soda water and tonic water, and no bar or bartender is credited with coining it.
pomada: Pomada is the drink of Menorca's summer fiestas, gin from Mahón mixed with cloudy lemonade, and its roots go back to the island's British occupation in the eighteenth century, when Royal Navy sailors created a demand for gin and local distillers began to make it. Menorcan gin, distilled from wine alcohol with juniper, has its own protected geographical indication as Gin de Mahón. In Ciutadella the mix is called gin amb llimonada, while elsewhere on the island it is pomada, a name that comes from the Xoriguer distillery's own bottled version.
agua-de-sevilla: Agua de Sevilla is a Seville bar drink of cava enriched with brandy, orange liqueur and pineapple under whipped cream, a local summer speciality whose creator and date are not recorded.
zurracapote: Zurracapote is a fiesta wine punch of La Rioja, red wine or clarete left to macerate with peaches, lemon, sugar and cinnamon, made by local festival clubs there and in neighbouring regions as far as Cuenca, and its beginnings are not documented.
sangria-blanca: Sangría Blanca is the white-wine version of sangría, the Spanish wine punch named from sangre, blood, for the colour of the red original, made lighter with dry white wine, peach, citrus and brandy, and it has no recorded creator.
kir-breton: The Kir Breton is Brittany's version of the Kir, the Burgundian aperitif of white wine and crème de cassis named after Félix Kir, the post-war mayor of Dijon, made instead with the region's dry cider.
trou-normand: The trou normand, the Norman hole, is the Normandy custom of taking a small glass of calvados partway through a long meal, on the old belief that it makes room for the courses still to come, a regional habit with no inventor that restaurants now often serve as apple sorbet doused in calvados.
bacardi-cocktail: Bacardí, the rum house Facundo Bacardí Massó founded in Santiago de Cuba, made its name with a lighter, filtered rum, and the cocktail named after it began as a Daiquiri of Bacardí, lime and sugar. The red version, coloured with grenadine, grew up in American bars. Its popularity led to a legal fight, and after the repeal of Prohibition the New York Supreme Court ruled that a drink sold as a Bacardi Cocktail had to be made with Bacardí rum, a rare case of a court tying a cocktail to a brand.
new-york-sour: Despite its name, the New York Sour is usually traced by drinks historians to Chicago in the 1880s, where a bartender is said to have finished a whiskey sour with a float of claret, and it circulated under other names, among them the Continental Sour, before settling on New York. The red wine is poured gently over the back of a spoon so that it sits as a separate layer, and the two parts are meant to be tasted together. The original bartender's name is not recorded. It is now an International Bartenders Association official cocktail.
spicy-fifty: Salvatore Calabrese, the Italian bartender long based in London, created the Spicy Fifty around 2005 as the signature drink of Fifty, a members' club in St James's that opened that February. It drew on the chilli-heavy cooking of the chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten, and the name joins the club's with the kick of fresh red chilli. Vanilla vodka, elderflower, honey and lime make up the rest of the drink. In 2020 the International Bartenders Association added it to its list of official cocktails in the New Era category.
spricer: The špricer is Slovenia's everyday mix of white wine and sparkling water, the same drink as the Austrian Gespritzter, the Hungarian fröccs and the Croatian gemišt, with a name from the German spritzen, to spray, and no recorded inventor.
southside-fizz: The Southside Fizz is the long version of the Southside, the gin, citrus, sugar and mint sour whose origin is disputed. One story links it to the Southside Sportsmen's Club on Long Island, another to Chicago's South Side, where Prohibition gangs are said to have needed mint and sugar to make rough gin palatable, a tale often dismissed as legend. New York's 21 Club made the Southside one of its house drinks and serves it with a splash of soda, which effectively makes it a fizz.
army-and-navy: The Army and Navy, gin with lemon and orgeat, was in print by 1948, when David Embury included it in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks. The name is often linked with the Army and Navy Club in Washington or with the annual Army-Navy football game, but neither connection has been documented, and no creator is recorded. Orgeat, an almond syrup traditionally scented with orange flower water, does the work that plain sugar would in most sours and adds body as well as sweetness, which gives the drink its fuller texture.
honeysuckle: The Honeysuckle is the Daiquiri of rum and lime made with honey in place of sugar, a close relative of the gin-based Bee's Knees, and no creator is recorded for it.
petite-fleur: The Petite Fleur, French for little flower, is an equal-parts mix of white rum, Cointreau and grapefruit juice in the old house style of equal measures, and no creator or date is recorded for it.
ideal-cocktail: The Ideal Cocktail is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, one of the early Martini variations that added fruit and a touch of liqueur to gin and vermouth. Here a spoonful of grapefruit juice and a few dashes of maraschino make the drink brighter and slightly bitter. Who named it the Ideal, and why, is not recorded, and it is rarely seen today outside classic-cocktail bars.
marmalade-cocktail: The Marmalade Cocktail appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, written as a recipe for a party of six: gin, lemon juice and a couple of spoonfuls of orange marmalade shaken together. Craddock noted that its bittersweet taste made it especially suitable as an aperitif before lunch. Marmalade, made from bitter Seville oranges, was a fixture of the British breakfast table, and the idea of shaking it into a gin drink returned decades later in Salvatore Calabrese's Breakfast Martini.
shamrock: The Shamrock appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, an Irish whiskey and dry vermouth drink tinted green with small amounts of green Chartreuse and crème de menthe, and named for the three-leafed plant that is Ireland's emblem and the symbol of St Patrick. It comes from a period when Irish whiskey was still widely poured in British and American bars, before the industry's long decline in the twentieth century. Its creator is not recorded, and it is most often made today around St Patrick's Day.
blarney-stone: The Blarney Stone, Irish whiskey seasoned with absinthe, curaçao and maraschino, is an old-style Irish whiskey cocktail named after the stone at Blarney Castle near Cork that visitors kiss for the gift of eloquence, and its creator is not recorded.
habushu: Habushu is an Okinawan liqueur of awamori, the rice spirit of the Ryukyu Islands, steeped with a habu pit viper and usually sweetened with honey and herbs, and when the practice began on Okinawa is not documented.
sodabi: Sodabi is Benin's palm-wine spirit, and the most widely cited account of its name credits the Sodabi brothers of Allada, two Beninese men who learned to distil while serving in French colonial regiments in the First World War. After returning home in 1918 they tried fermented bananas and pineapples before settling on palm wine, and the method spread through Benin and Togo in the 1930s despite a colonial ban. A popular story that an Englishman exclaimed so that be on tasting it is generally dismissed.
klekovaca: Klekovača is a western Balkan plum brandy distilled or redistilled with juniper berries, named from kleka, a local word for juniper, and it comes from a rural tradition with no single recorded origin.
chinguirito: Chinguirito is the cane spirit of colonial New Spain, distilled from sugarcane juice, molasses or piloncillo, and its history is largely a history of prohibition. The Spanish Crown banned cane spirit in its American colonies for much of the colonial period to protect sales of brandy shipped from Spain, and chinguirito was made in secret along the Gulf coast around Veracruz and elsewhere. The Crown finally legalised it, and began taxing it, at the end of the eighteenth century. The origin of the name has not been documented.
chuchuhuasi: Chuchuhuasi is the bark of an Amazonian tree and, in Peru, the drink made by steeping that bark in cane aguardiente with honey, sold in Amazon cities such as Iquitos, and no date or originator is recorded.
yaa-dong: Yaa dong, roughly steeped medicine in Thai, is the roadside custom of steeping roots, bark and herbs in lao khao rice spirit in big glass jars, each vendor keeping its own blend, with no recorded beginning.
pox: Pox, pronounced posh, is the ceremonial spirit of the Maya communities of the Chiapas highlands, distilled from maize and sugarcane and offered in churches such as San Juan Chamula's, and when distilling began there is not documented.
ruby-port: Port took shape in the seventeenth century, when English merchants shipping wine from Portugal's Douro valley found that adding grape brandy kept it sound on the voyage, and in 1756 the Marquis of Pombal made the Douro one of the first legally demarcated wine regions in the world. Fortification happens during fermentation: grape spirit of about 77 per cent is added to stop the yeast and keep the wine's natural sugar. Ruby is the youngest and simplest expression of the style, aged only a few years in large vats so that it keeps its colour and fresh fruit.
tawny-port: Tawny Port is the Douro's long-aged style, the same fortified wine as ruby but left for years in small oak casks, where slow oxidation fades the colour from red to amber and brings out nutty, caramel flavours. The Douro was demarcated in 1756, among the first wine regions to be legally defined, and its shippers, many of them British houses with Portuguese lodges in Vila Nova de Gaia, blended aged tawnies as their house styles. Indicated-age tawnies, labelled 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old, describe the average character of the blend rather than the age of its youngest wine.
vintage-port: Vintage Port is the Douro's single-harvest wine, made only in years that a house judges exceptional and formally declares, which historically has happened only a few times a decade. After about two years in cask it is bottled unfiltered to age for decades in glass, throwing a heavy sediment that makes decanting necessary. The style depends on bottles that can be laid on their side, and it developed in the eighteenth century as shippers began to bottle and cellar their best years, a practice that built the reputation of port's old British houses.
amontillado-sherry: Amontillado takes its name from Montilla, the town south of Córdoba whose wines it was originally meant to resemble: amontillado means in the style of Montilla. In the bodegas of Jerez it describes a sherry that begins under flor, the protective yeast that shapes fino, and then, once the flor dies away or is ended with further fortification, continues to age in contact with air, gaining colour and nutty depth. The style was well established by the nineteenth century, when Edgar Allan Poe made a cask of it the bait in his tale The Cask of Amontillado.
cream-sherry: Cream sherry was created in the cellars of John Harvey & Sons in Bristol, a city that had long imported sweet sherry blends known as Bristol Milk. From the 1860s Harvey's sons developed a richer blend sweetened with Pedro Ximénez, and the company's story holds that a visiting lady, offered it after the familiar Bristol Milk, declared that if that was milk, this must be cream. Harveys Bristol Cream became the firm's flagship and, from the late 1920s, a major export to the United States.
fino-sherry: Fino is the driest and palest style of sherry, and its character comes from flor, a layer of yeast that grows naturally on the surface of young wine in the cool, humid bodegas of the Jerez region. Under flor the wine is shielded from air while the yeast consumes glycerine and residual sugar, leaving it lean, saline and almond-scented. Fino rose to prominence in the nineteenth century as shippers came to value the flor-aged wines, and in the twentieth century Jerez became the first official denominación de origen in Spain.
manzanilla-sherry: Manzanilla is the fino of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, and by law it can only be aged there. The town's damp Atlantic air keeps the flor yeast thick and active all year, which gives manzanilla a lighter, more saline character than the finos of Jerez. Its name, which is also the Spanish word for chamomile, has been explained both by the wine's aroma and by the village of Manzanilla in Huelva, and the question has never been settled. It has its own denominación, separate from Jerez.
oloroso-sherry: Oloroso, Spanish for scented, is the sherry made to age without flor. In the bodegas of Jerez the cellar master selects fuller-bodied young wines and fortifies them to around 17 per cent or more, too strong for the protective yeast to survive, so the wine ages in contact with air from the start. Over years in the solera, the system of stacked casks that blends older and younger wines, it darkens and gains walnut and dried-fruit depth. Olorosos are naturally dry, and they are the base of sweetened blends such as cream sherry.
palo-cortado-sherry: Palo cortado is the sherry that does not follow its plan. It begins as a fine young wine destined for fino or amontillado, but for reasons cellar masters have never fully explained, the flor fades and the wine starts to develop more like an oloroso while keeping some of its original finesse. The name, cut stick, comes from the chalk marks used in the bodegas of Jerez: a single vertical stroke, or palo, marks a cask headed for the fino style, and when the wine changes course the cellar master strikes a line across it. True palo cortado is rare.
pedro-ximenez-sherry: Pedro Ximénez is both a grape and the sweetest of sherry's styles. Legend holds that the grape was brought to Andalusia in the sixteenth century by a soldier named Pieter Siemens, returning from the Rhine or the Canary Islands, though the story is unproven. The grapes are laid out to dry in the sun until they are close to raisins, then pressed, and the thick, dark wine can carry well over 400 grams of sugar per litre. Its heartland is Montilla-Moriles, but Jerez bodegas age it in their soleras too, and in Spain it is often poured over vanilla ice cream.
dry-vermouth: Dry vermouth was born in Lyon in 1813, when the herbalist Joseph Noilly created a pale, dry formula that became the first French vermouth, a counterpart to the sweet red style of Turin. Noilly is said to have modelled it on the way wine changes during long sea voyages, and his son Louis and son-in-law Claudius Prat later moved production to Marseillan on the Mediterranean coast, founding Noilly Prat in 1855. Chambéry's Dolin followed with its own dry and blanc styles, and French dry vermouth became the classic partner for gin in the dry Martini.
sweet-vermouth: Modern vermouth began in Turin in 1786, when Antonio Benedetto Carpano, working in a liquor shop near the royal palace, sold a sweetened wine flavoured with wormwood and other botanicals and called it vermouth, after Wermut, the German for wormwood. It quickly found favour at the Savoy court, and Turin became the capital of the sweet Italian style, home to Martini & Rossi, Cinzano and Carpano's own Antica Formula. Through the nineteenth century Italian vermouth crossed to American bars, where it became essential to the Manhattan and later to the Negroni.
lions-tail: The Lion's Tail is printed in the Café Royal Cocktail Book, compiled by W. J. Tarling and published in London in 1937, one of the few bourbon drinks in a British bar book of the period. Its name borrows a nineteenth-century American expression: twisting the lion's tail meant provoking Britain, whose royal arms bear a lion, which has led drinks historians to suspect an American contributor working in London after Prohibition. The drink was largely forgotten until Ted Haigh revived it in his book Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, just as allspice dram was returning to American shelves.
million-dollar-cocktail: The Million Dollar Cocktail is traditionally credited to Ngiam Tong Boon, the Hainanese bartender at the Long Bar of the Raffles Hotel in Singapore in the early twentieth century, who is also credited with the Singapore Sling, although the documentary evidence for both attributions is thin and drinks historians have questioned them. Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book, which carried it to a wider audience in London. Its egg white gives it a thick foam that set it apart from most gin and vermouth drinks of the period.
maximilian-affair: The Maximilian Affair is credited to Misty Kalkofen, who created it in 2008 while tending bar at Green Street in Cambridge, Massachusetts, part of the Boston bar scene that helped bring mezcal into American cocktails. The name nods to France's intervention in Mexico, when Napoleon III installed the Austrian archduke Maximilian as emperor: French elderflower liqueur meets Mexican mezcal, with Italian Punt e Mes as a third party and lemon to hold them together.
east-india-cocktail: The East India Cocktail first appears in Harry Johnson's Bartender's Manual of 1882, where Johnson, a German-born New York bartender, noted that it was a great favourite with the English living in the different parts of East India. His brandy-based recipe used curaçao, maraschino, a fruit syrup and bitters, and the drink drifted as it was copied: Johnson adjusted it in later editions, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 printed a version with pineapple juice. Who first mixed it, and where, is not recorded.
up-to-date: The Up-to-Date comes from Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks, published in New York in 1916 by the head bartender of the Hotel Wallick on Times Square. Ensslin's book was one of the last American bar guides before Prohibition closed the country's saloons, and it is also the first known printing of the Aviation. The Up-to-Date's pairing of whiskey and sherry in equal measure was largely forgotten until the classic-cocktail revival, when bartenders rediscovered sherry as a mixer and went back to Ensslin's pages for recipes.
old-hickory: The Old Hickory is recorded in Stanley Clisby Arthur's Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em, published in 1937, where Arthur tells the story that it was a favourite of General Andrew Jackson, nicknamed Old Hickory, during the defence of New Orleans against the British in the winter of 1814 and 1815. The anecdote is unverified, and Arthur's book is known for colourful stories, but the drink itself, built entirely on two vermouths and two bitters, is a genuine New Orleans classic and one of the lowest-strength drinks in the city's canon.
cherry-blossom: The Cherry Blossom is generally credited to Tasaburo Tao of Bar Paris in Yokohama, who created it in the 1920s, and it is one of the earliest Japanese cocktails to win fame abroad, appearing in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book in London in 1930. Yokohama, the treaty port where foreign residents and hotel bars introduced Western drinking to Japan, had already produced the Bamboo, created at the city's Grand Hotel by Louis Eppinger. Tao's drink was built and coloured to recall the sakura, the cherry blossom of the Japanese spring.
yokohama: The Yokohama Cocktail was in print by 1930, when Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book, and it is named after the Japanese treaty port where Western-style hotel bars first took root in Japan. It is an unusual drink for its time, combining gin with vodka, still rare in British and American bars, along with orange juice and grenadine. Its creator is not recorded, and whether it was devised in Yokohama itself or simply named after the city by a bartender elsewhere is unknown.
joy-division: Phil Ward created the Joy Division at Death & Co in New York's East Village in the late 2000s, before he left to open Mayahuel, his agave-focused bar. He started from a dry gin Martini and added Cointreau and a few dashes of absinthe, a small change that makes the drink brighter and more aromatic without hiding the gin. Its name borrows that of the Manchester post-punk band.
paper-tiger: The Paper Tiger is a modern Negroni variation that keeps the equal measures of Campari and sweet vermouth and swaps gin for spiced dark rum, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.
brainstorm: The Brainstorm is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930: Irish whiskey stirred with two dashes each of Bénédictine and French vermouth and finished with orange peel. It is one of the few classic cocktails built on Irish whiskey rather than rye or bourbon, from a period when Irish whiskey was still widely poured in American and British bars. Who created it, and where its name came from, is not recorded.
fog-horn: The Fog Horn, gin and lime lengthened with ginger, is an early member of the buck family, the highballs of spirit, citrus and ginger ale or ginger beer that took shape in American bars around the turn of the twentieth century. It is recorded among the drinks of the original Waldorf-Astoria bar in New York, whose recipes were collected by Albert Stevens Crockett, and it predates the Moscow Mule, which applied the same structure to vodka, by decades. Its creator is not recorded, and neither is the reason for its name.
blue-train: The Blue Train is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, a gin sour with Cointreau and lemon named after the Calais-Mediterranean Express, the luxury overnight sleeper to the Riviera known as Le Train Bleu for its blue-and-gold carriages. The train was a symbol of the 1920s smart set, celebrated in a Diaghilev ballet and an Agatha Christie novel. Craddock coloured the drink with a dash of blue vegetable extract, the job blue curaçao does in most later versions, and its creator is not recorded.
prince-edward: The Prince Edward is a Scotch cocktail built like a Bobby Burns, with Drambuie and Lillet in place of the vermouth, and which Prince Edward it honours, and who first mixed it, are not recorded.
la-perla: La Perla is credited to Jacques Bezuidenhout, the South African-born bartender based in San Francisco, who paired reposado tequila with manzanilla sherry and a measure of pear liqueur. It is usually linked to Tres Agaves, the tequila-focused restaurant and bar where he worked in the city, and it became one of the best-known sherry cocktails of the American revival. Its saline edge comes from the manzanilla, aged under flor, a living cap of yeast that keeps air away from the wine.
ferrari: The Ferrari, equal parts Fernet-Branca and Campari, joins two of Milan's best-known bitters in a bartenders' pour that rarely reaches a printed menu, and it has no recorded creator or date, its name usually explained by its racing-red colour.
boomerang: The Boomerang appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, a whisky drink made there with Canadian Club, dry vermouth and Swedish punsch, sharpened with dashes of bitters and lemon. Swedish punsch traces its beginnings to 1733, when the Swedish East India Company's ships began bringing Batavia arrack to Gothenburg, and it was common enough in London bars between the wars that the Savoy used it without explanation. It then all but vanished from English-speaking bars for decades, and the Boomerang's creator is not recorded.
